<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
# Restatement

The comment re-analyses the Halden microdata and identifies four problems.

1. **Attrition.** Seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule began, not during preparation as the working paper states. Six of the nine cited workload or inability to maintain output; two cited scheduling.
2. **Output.** For the 23 organisations that submitted records, the manager-reported index exceeds the record-based index by 3.8 points (98.9 against 95.1), and it is higher in 19 of the 23.
3. **Hours.** Time-tracking logs from 27 organisations show actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%, because of longer remaining days and work on the day off. In the 17 organisations with both records and logs, the gain per actual hour is 10.8% rather than 23.4%.
4. **Revenue.** Deflated by 4.1% consumer price inflation, the reported +1.4% becomes a real fall of about 2.6%.

The comment then argues three further points:

- Per-hour gains in every sector are an artifact of the metric. Retail output fell 11.2% in the three retail organisations with records, which fits the Varden counter result.
- The remaining roughly 11% is plausibly a novelty effect, because self-reported energy decays from month three to month six.
- The Varden meetings analysis is a post hoc subgroup finding that should not be cited.

It concludes that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty." The data note concedes that the corrected subsets are not random samples of the pilot.

# Assessment

Sections 1 to 5 are valuable and mostly sound. Sections 6 to 8 go beyond what the evidence supports, and the conclusion contradicts the comment's own numbers. The Halden paper inflated its result. This comment corrects that and then overcorrects into the opposite error.

## What holds up

- **Attrition (section 1)** is the most important finding. It contradicts a factual statement in the working paper, and the Halden authors should correct the record. I had guessed the withdrawals were coverage-related; the microdata point more broadly to output problems.
- **The arithmetic checks out:**
  - 98.9 − 95.1 = 3.8.
  - 40.3 → 34.6 is −14.1%, and 40.4 → 34.8 is −13.9%.
  - 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6%, and 95.4 / 0.861 = +10.8%.
  - 1.014 / 1.041 gives a real change of −2.6%.
- **The direction of each correction is well evidenced.** Nineteen of 23 managers rated output above their own records, and the time-tracking logs measure hours directly.
- **The sectoral critique (section 5)** is correct, and the recommendations in section 8 are good.

## Problems

**1. The conclusion contradicts the evidence the comment presents.**

- The comment's own best estimate, from record-based output and actual hours, is a 10.8% gain per hour. It is not zero.
- The Varden case-processing stratum is randomised, uses administrative output and timesheet hours, and found +12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4).
- The comment calls Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature" but never mentions the case-processing result from the same trial, which has 14 offices against the counter stratum's 10. Citing one stratum as decisive while omitting the other is selective.
- "Entirely an artifact" therefore rests on the novelty argument alone, and that argument is open (see point 3). A defensible conclusion would read:

  > "corrected gains are roughly half those reported; whether the remainder persists is unknown."

**2. The abstract claims attrition was corrected, but Table 2 does not correct for it.**

- The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems, including attrition, brings the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 adjusts only output and hours.
- Attrition is never quantified. A bounds analysis would do this by assigning the nine withdrawers plausible worst-case and neutral outcomes.
- The abstract should either describe Table 2 accurately or the paper should add that analysis.

**3. The novelty argument is weaker than presented.**

- **The arithmetic is off.** A linear fit through 0.61 at month 3 and 0.29 at month 6 declines by about 0.107 per month. That reaches zero around month 8.7, not month 10.
- **Two points cannot fix a trajectory.** A line through two observations cannot distinguish a return to baseline from levelling off at a new, higher plateau.
- **Energy is not output.** The comment infers that output gains decay from a decline in self-reported energy. The Halden index was collected monthly, so the comment could test directly whether output per hour declined over the six months, and it doesn't.
- **Varden partly addresses novelty.** Its effect was measured at nine months, against a randomised control whose staff also knew a trial was under way. That does not rule novelty out, but it bears on the question.
- **The burden-of-proof framing closes an open question.** "Six months is not long enough to distinguish" is a correct statement that the question is open. "Entirely an artifact" treats the same question as settled.

**4. The criticism of the Varden meetings analysis attacks claims the Varden authors did not make.**

- The Varden authors did not present meetings as a mechanism. They wrote that a correlation across seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," labelled the analysis unregistered, and registered a confirmatory test.
- The seven offices are the treated arm of a pre-specified stratum, not a subgroup chosen afterwards.
- The meeting data were collected at month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results were known.
- "Should not be cited as a mechanism" is fair. "Post hoc account fitted to a subgroup" misdescribes what was done.

**5. Table 2 changes the sample at the same time as the correction.**

- Its rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations, so each step mixes the effect of the correction with the effect of switching to a different subset of organisations.
- The cleaner presentation keeps the sample fixed. For the 17 organisations, it would report all four specifications: manager-reported output with scheduled hours, then each correction separately, then both together.
- The final estimate also needs a confidence interval. With 17 organisations, 10.8% may be compatible with a wide range.

**6. The breakdown of hours doesn't add up.**

- Baseline was about 8.1 hours a day over five days. The 32 scheduled hours imply about 8 a day over four days.
- Adding 0.7 hours to each of four days and 1.6 hours on the day off gives roughly 36.4 hours a week, not the reported 34.6.
- The figures fit if the 0.7 is per week rather than per day: 32 + 0.7 + 1.6 = 34.3. One of the components appears to have the wrong unit.

**7. Smaller points**

- **Retail.** The 11.2% fall rests on three organisations. That is consistent with Varden's counter result but is not independent confirmation of it.
- **Revenue.** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, and without a comparison group the real −2.6% shows only that revenue did not grow in real terms, not that the pilot caused a decline. The comment's criticism of the "growth" framing is right; the figure doesn't support more than that.

# Where the evidence across the three documents stands

| Status | Finding |
|---|---|
| Found | Halden's 23.4% overstates the per-hour gain. Correcting output and hours roughly halves it, to about 11% in the subset where both corrections are possible. |
| Found | Halden's account of the withdrawals was inaccurate, and the withdrawals were related to output. |
| Found | Where output depends on staff presence, reduced hours reduce output and service. |
| Found (one randomised trial, nine months) | In backlog work, output per employee held within about 7%, and output per actual hour rose by about 12%. |
| Open | Whether per-hour gains persist beyond 6 to 9 months. |
| Open | How much of the gain comes from cutting low-value time, such as meetings, rather than from rest. |
| Open | How large the attrition bias in the Halden pilot is. |

If useful, I can draft a response letter to the comment from either side, or sketch the attrition bounds analysis and the fixed-sample version of Table 2.
